children: Vicor
surged about 12% in extended trading Monday after the power technology company sharply raised its third-quarter revenue growth outlook, citing royalties from a recently announced licensing agreement.
The Andover, Massachusetts-based company said it now expects third-quarter revenue to grow more than 20% sequentially, compared with its previous forecast for growth of nearly 10%.
Vicor
attributed the improved outlook to royalties from a recently announced non-exclusive license for its Vertical Power Delivery, or VPD, technology.

The guidance increase implies third-quarter growth will be at least twice the rate Vicor previously expected. The announcement also gives investors a clearer indication that intellectual-property licensing could become a more meaningful contributor to the company's financial results.
Licensing strategy takes shape

Chief Executive Patrizio Vinciarelli said four leading companies among original equipment manufacturers and hyperscalers have secured licenses to power-system technology developed and patented by Vicor.
Vinciarelli said other hyperscalers have contacted Vicor following intellectual-property disputes involving computing systems and the company's technology.

Vicor is seeking to monetize patents covering technology used to deliver power to high-performance computing systems. Demand for power-efficient infrastructure has become increasingly important as hyperscalers deploy more power-intensive artificial intelligence accelerators and other advanced computing hardware.
The company indicated it is pursuing a licensing model that allows suppliers to sell power modules incorporating Vicor's patented technology to licensed OEMs and hyperscalers.
Patent enforcement remains part of strategy
Vicor
also reiterated that it intends to enforce its intellectual-property rights against companies it believes are infringing its patents.
The company said suppliers that sell allegedly infringing products without appropriate licenses could face monetary damages or restrictions on selling products covered by Vicor patents.

Those statements represent Vicor's position on its intellectual-property rights and don't by themselves establish that particular suppliers have infringed its patents. Patent disputes can involve lengthy litigation and uncertain outcomes.
The immediate catalyst for Vicor

shares is the magnitude of the guidance revision. Moving from nearly 10% sequential revenue growth to more than 20% suggests the recently announced royalty agreement is having a material effect on third-quarter results.

Potentially more important is whether the latest agreement can be replicated. If additional hyperscalers and suppliers license Vicor's VPD patents, licensing revenue could supplement sales of the company's power modules without requiring a corresponding increase in manufacturing volume.

That also makes the number and economics of future licenses important metrics for investors to watch. Vicor didn't disclose the royalty rate or quantify how much of its revised third-quarter outlook comes from the new agreement.

The 12% after-hours gain suggests investors initially viewed the announcement as evidence that Vicor's patent portfolio may have greater earnings potential than previously reflected in expectations. The durability of that benefit will depend on additional licensing agreements, royalty revenue and the company's ability to defend its intellectual property.
